title: Perceived leadership effectiveness
instructions: Think about how this person behaved in the meeting you just had. Please answer to what extent you perceive this person as effective if they were your own leader.
anchors: not at all effective as a leader
citation: Sheng, Andrews & van Vugt (2026), Study 5, Sample E. The operative question and the anchors are theirs verbatim: 'to what extent you perceive these leadership descriptions as effective if these individuals were your own leaders… (1 = not at all effective as a leader, 7 = extremely effective as a leader)'. Only the stimulus differs, and deliberately.
note:
The paper's effectiveness measure IS this question and this 1-7 scale; its 57 items are the STIMULI, not the criterion — twelve published leadership-style scales (Cheng et al. 2004/2014; Wang & Howell 2010; Bai et al. 2020; Hu et al. 2025; Back et al. 2013) reworded as descriptions of hypothetical leaders, each style's 4-6 descriptions averaged into one score. Here the stimulus is a specific agent the respondent has just watched for three rounds, which is the gap the study exists to address: no participant in their Study 5 ever observed anyone.

The real cost of that substitution is reliability, not provenance. Their score for a style averages 4-6 ratings, so it has an alpha; one rating of one person does not, and none can be computed for this instrument. Multiple stimuli per style has no analogue when the stimulus is a single observed person, so this is not fixable by adding paraphrased items — those would measure agreement between rewordings, not between observations.

A second cost: their dominance-side null is specific to Authoritarianism, Narcissism and Dominance as separate scales, while protection -> Safety is .43***/.20***, strongly supported. One rating of one person cannot separate those, so H5's replication here is of a construct this design collapses.

effectiveness: Indicate your perception of this person's effectiveness as a leader.
